claim: Running stably on uneven natural terrain was critical for human evolution.
source: Running stably on uneven natural terrain takes skillful control and was critical for human evolution.
evidence: Supported by citations to evolutionary literature in the introduction section.

claim: Runners do not selectively step on more level ground areas on uneven terrain.
source: We find that runners do not selectively step on more level ground areas.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of footstep patterns and comparison with directed and blind sampling schemes.

claim: The body's mechanical response, mediated by the control of leg compliance, helps maintain stability without requiring precise regulation of footsteps.
source: Instead, the body's mechanical response, mediated by the control of leg compliance, helps maintain stability without requiring precise regulation of footsteps.
evidence: Supported by collision model analysis and experimental measurements of fore-aft impulses.

claim: Overall kinematics and energy consumption on uneven terrain showed little change from flat ground.
source: Furthermore, their overall kinematics and energy consumption on uneven terrain showed little change from flat ground.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of metabolic rate and kinematic variables across terrain types.

claim: Mathematical modeling predicts that even slightly uneven ground could be severely destabilizing unless some form of mitigation strategy is employed.
source: Mathematical modeling predicts that even slightly uneven ground, with peak-to-valley height variations less than the dorso-plantar foot height, could be severely destabilizing unless some form of mitigation strategy is employed to deal with them (Dhawale et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical modeling work.

claim: Footsteps are visually guided to plan a path through complex, uneven terrain in human walking.
source: Studies on human walking find that footsteps are visually guided to plan a path through complex, uneven terrain (Matthis et al., 2018; Thomas et al., 2020; Bonnen et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to walking studies.

claim: Vision is needed to track footprints and continuously survey the landscape for prey in persistence hunting.
source: For example, in the evolutionary context of persistence hunting (Carrier et al., 1984; Bramble and Lieberman, 2004), vision is needed to track footprints and continuously survey the landscape for prey in addition to dealing with the terrain's unevenness.
evidence: Supported by citations to evolutionary literature and logical inference about visual demands.

claim: Random variations in slope lead to step-to-step fluctuations in the fore-aft ground impulse.
source: The mathematical analyses of Dhawale et al., 2019, find that random variations in slope lead to step-to-step fluctuations in the fore-aft ground impulse.
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical analysis.

claim: Small step-to-step random variation of the fore-aft ground impulse leads to a gradual accumulation of sagittal plane angular momentum, which ultimately destabilizes the runner.
source: But small step-to-step random variation of the fore-aft ground impulse leads to a gradual accumulation of sagittal plane angular momentum, which ultimately destabilizes the runner.
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical analysis (Dhawale et al., 2019).

claim: All subjects were able-bodied, ran approximately 30 km per week, and had run at least one half-marathon or marathon within the previous year.
source: All subjects were able-bodied, ran approximately 30 km per week, and had run at least one half-marathon or marathon within the previous year.
evidence: Direct statement of subject characteristics.

claim: Subjects ran back-and-forth on three 24 m long and 0.6 m wide tracks.
source: Subjects ran back-and-forth on three 24 m long and 0.6 m wide tracks (Figure 2a).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental setup with reference to figure.

claim: Kinematics were recorded using an 8-camera motion capture system at 300 frames per second.
source: We recorded kinematics using an 8-camera motion capture system (Vicon Inc., Oxford, UK) at 300 frames per second and measured the ground reaction forces at 600 Hz using two force plates (AMTI Inc., model BP600900) embedded beneath the center of the track.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental methods.

claim: Ground reaction forces were measured at 600 Hz using two force plates.
source: We recorded kinematics using an 8-camera motion capture system (Vicon Inc., Oxford, UK) at 300 frames per second and measured the ground reaction forces at 600 Hz using two force plates (AMTI Inc., model BP600900) embedded beneath the center of the track.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental methods.

claim: Subjects ran at a controlled speed of 3 m/s.
source: We controlled the running speed using a moving light array in 24 m long LED strips laid on either side of the track (Figure 2a). Subjects were instructed to stay within the bounds of a 3 m illuminated segment of the LED strip that traveled at 3 m/s.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental protocol.

claim: The speed of 3 m/s was chosen as it was comfortable for all subjects and lies within the endurance running speed range for humans.
source: This speed was chosen as it was comfortable for all subjects and lies within the endurance running speed range for humans (Bramble and Lieberman, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation and experimental observation.

claim: All participants were heel-strike runners on all terrain types.
source: All participants were heel-strike runners on all terrain types, as judged from the double peak in the vertical ground reaction force profile.
evidence: Supported by analysis of ground reaction force data.

claim: The directed scheme finds substantially more level landing patches than human runners.
source: However, the directed scheme finds substantially more level landing patches, showing that it was possible for the runners to land on more level ground (directed scheme in Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The variability of the fore-aft impulse is just 1% of the forward momentum.
source: The low variability of the fore-aft impulse, just 1% of the forward momentum, suggests that it is tightly regulated across runners, terrain, and steps.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements.

claim: Runners rely on their body's passive mechanical response for remaining stable on undulating uneven terrain rather than vision-based path planning.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that runners rely not on vision-based path planning, but on their body's passive mechanical response for remaining stable on undulating uneven terrain.
evidence: Inferred from experimental findings on footstep patterns and fore-aft impulses.

claim: Low joint stiffness underlies the regulation of fore-aft impulses.
source: Based on the modeling estimate of collisional impulses and comparison with measurements, we propose that low joint stiffness underlie the regulation of fore-aft impulses, likely contributing to stability (Dhawale et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by collision model analysis compared with experimental measurements and theoretical predictions.

claim: The measured fore-aft impulses were partly consistent with an idealized extreme of zero stiffness in the joints at the point of landing.
source: By examining the role of leg joint compliance using model-based analyses of the data, we found that the measured fore-aft impulses were partly consistent with an idealized extreme of zero stiffness in the joints at the point of landing.
evidence: Supported by comparison of experimental data with collision model predictions.

claim: The compliant model's predicted fore-aft impulses show good agreement with measurements when the impulse is below 0.07.
source: The compliant model's predicted fore-aft impulses show good agreement with measurements when the impulse is below 0.07 (measured versus predicted in Figure 6d), and disagree only for the occasional steps when runners experience more severe fore-aft impulses.
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental measurements shown in Figure 6d.

claim: The stiff model consistently over-estimates the measured fore-aft impulse over its entire range.
source: Unlike the compliant model, the stiff model consistently over-estimates the measured fore-aft impulse over its entire range.
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental measurements.

claim: Maintaining low joint stiffness at landing helps maintain low fore-aft impulses despite variations in touchdown foot speed.
source: Thus, we propose that maintaining low joint stiffness at landing helps maintain low fore-aft impulses despite variations in touchdown foot speed.
evidence: Inferred from collision model analysis and experimental measurements.

claim: If the dimensionless forward foot speed at landing varied through its entire observed range from −0.2 to 1.1, it would result in a change in landing angle of 0.08 rad or 5°.
source: If the dimensionless forward foot speed at landing varied through its entire observed range from −0.2 to 1.1, it would result in a change in landing angle of 0.08 rad or 5°.
evidence: Calculated from the statistical relationship between foot speed and landing angle.

claim: The directed scheme exhibited decreased variability in step length and step width compared with the experimental data.
source: The directed scheme found more level patches and exhibited decreased variability in step length and step width compared with the experimental data.
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental measurements.

claim: The standard deviation of step length decreased by 80% on both uneven I and uneven II for the directed scheme compared to experimental measurements.
source: However, the standard deviation of step length decreased by 80% on both uneven I and uneven II compared to experimental measurements.
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental measurements.

claim: The standard deviation of step width for the directed scheme decreased by 80% on uneven I and by 84% on uneven II compared to experimental measurements.
source: The standard deviation of step width for the directed scheme decreased by 80% (0.0006 m) on uneven I and by 84% (0.005 m) on uneven II compared to experimental measurements.
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental measurements.

claim: The models at the two extremes of joint stiffness bound the experimental data, with the compliant model underestimating the measured fore-aft impulse while the stiff model overestimates it.
source: The models at the two extremes of joint stiffness bound the experimental data, with the compliant model underestimating the measured fore-aft impulse while the stiff model overestimates it (Figure 6c, d, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: There is no change in the variability of the leg landing angle between flat and uneven terrain trials.
source: For example, we see no change in the variability of the leg landing angle between flat and uneven terrain trials (Table 2), which is expected if leg landing angle responded to variations in terrain height (Blum et al., 2014; Birn-Jeffery et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Table 2.

claim: There is a slight decrease in the virtual leg length at touchdown on the most uneven terrain compared to flat, but the difference is only around 1% of the leg length.
source: We find a slight decrease in the virtual leg length at touchdown on the most uneven terrain compared to flat, but the difference was only around 1% of the leg length (Table 2), whose effect on stability would be negligible.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Table 2.

claim: Higher leg retraction rates are found on uneven terrain.
source: We find higher leg retraction rates on uneven terrain, as also reported in running birds (Birn-Jeffery and Daley, 2012; Blum et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements and comparison with cited literature.

claim: There is only a weak dependence between leg retraction rate and leg touchdown angles.
source: However, we find only a weak dependence between leg retraction rate and leg touchdown angles.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements.

claim: Step width variability increased by 24% on uneven terrain compared to flat.
source: Like those studies, we find 24% greater step width variability on uneven terrain compared to flat, but no significant changes in step length variability (Figure 7b, Table 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 7b and Table 2.

claim: There are no significant changes in step length variability on uneven terrain compared to flat.
source: Like those studies, we find 24% greater step width variability on uneven terrain compared to flat, but no significant changes in step length variability (Figure 7b, Table 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 7b and Table 2.

claim: The median step width increased on uneven terrain by 13%.
source: We additionally find that the median step width increased on uneven terrain by 13%.
evidence: Calculated from experimental measurements.

claim: The stochastic stepping model was able to consistently find landing locations with lower unevenness than the human subjects.
source: The stochastic stepping model was able to consistently find landing locations with lower unevenness than the human subjects, while matching the measured mean stepping statistics and even reducing step-to-step variability, thus showing that the absence of a foot placement strategy was not due to a lack of feasible landing locations.
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental measurements.

claim: Reducing tangential collisions and maintaining low fore-aft impulses reduces the risk of falling by tumbling in the sagittal-plane.
source: A previous theoretical analysis hypothesized that reducing tangential collisions and maintaining low fore-aft impulses reduces the risk of falling by tumbling in the sagittal-plane (Dhawale et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical analysis.

claim: By employing leg compliance to reduce the fore-aft impulse, the runners could deal with stability independent of foot speed regulation for safety and comfort.
source: Thus, by employing leg compliance to reduce the fore-aft impulse, the runners could deal with stability independent of foot speed regulation for safety and comfort.
evidence: Inferred from experimental findings and comparison with bird studies.

claim: The peak-to-peak height variation of the terrain was less than 6% of the leg length.
source: Furthermore, the peak-to-peak height variation of our terrain was less than 6% of the leg length, unlike Blum et al., 2014 and Birn-Jeffery et al., 2014, who used larger step-like obstacles of 10% leg length or more.
evidence: Calculated from terrain measurements and subject leg length.

claim: Large step-like obstacles probably induce different swing-leg control strategies compared with undulating terrain with smaller height variations.
source: So large step-like obstacles probably induce different swing-leg control strategies compared with undulating terrain with smaller height variations.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of current results with previous studies.

claim: The increase in median step width on uneven terrain could be due to lateral stability challenges of running on relatively more complex terrain with smoothly varying slope and height variations in all directions.
source: The increase in median step width that we measure could be due to lateral stability challenges of running on relatively more complex terrain with smoothly varying slope and height variations in all directions.
evidence: Speculative explanation for experimental observation.

claim: The mean increase in metabolic power consumption of around 5% on uneven terrain is similar to Voloshina and Ferris, 2015.
source: Unlike treadmill running studies, we do not find a statistically significant increase in metabolic power consumption on uneven terrain versus flat ground, but the mean increase of around 5% is similar to Voloshina and Ferris, 2015.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements and comparison with cited literature.

claim: Foot placement strategies are used for obstacle avoidance on more complex terrain while the terrains in this study were designed to be continuously undulating and not have large, singular obstacles.
source: We speculate that foot placement strategies are used for obstacle avoidance (Matthis and Fajen, 2014) on more complex terrain while our terrains were designed to be continuously undulating and not have large, singular obstacles.
evidence: Speculative explanation based on comparison with cited literature.

claim: There is a possibility that there is a skill-learning component to terrain-guided foot placement strategies which could not be measured since the volunteers were not experienced trail runners.
source: While our data suggest that terrain-guided foot placement strategies are not required for stability on gently undulating terrain, it leaves open the possibility that there is a skill-learning component to such foot placement strategies which we could not measure since our volunteers were not experienced trail runners.
evidence: Speculative consideration of alternative explanation.

claim: The limited need for visual attention may explain how runners could employ vision for other functional goals, such as planning a path around large obstacles, or in an evolutionary context, tracking footprints to hunt prey on uneven terrain without falling.
source: The limited need for visual attention may explain how runners could employ vision for other functional goals, such as planning a path around large obstacles, or in an evolutionary context, tracking footprints to hunt prey on uneven terrain without falling.
evidence: Inferred from experimental findings about lack of vision-guided footstep regulation.

claim: Data from galloping dogs show that they do not alter their gait on uneven terrain.
source: Whether other animals employ similar strategies on uneven terrain is presently unknown but data from galloping dogs show that they do not alter their gait on uneven terrain (Wilshin et al., 2020), thus suggesting that other adept runners potentially employ similar principles for stability.
evidence: Supported by citation to dog running study.

claim: Other adept runners potentially employ similar principles for stability as human runners on uneven terrain.
source: Whether other animals employ similar strategies on uneven terrain is presently unknown but data from galloping dogs show that they do not alter their gait on uneven terrain (Wilshin et al., 2020), thus suggesting that other adept runners potentially employ similar principles for stability.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with dog running data.

claim: The results could translate to new strategies for reducing the real-time image processing burden in robotic systems.
source: We propose that our results could translate to new strategies for reducing the real-time image processing burden in robotic systems, and could also help in training trail runners by emphasizing limber joints when dealing with uneven terrain.
evidence: Speculative application of findings.

claim: The results could help in training trail runners by emphasizing limber joints when dealing with uneven terrain.
source: We propose that our results could translate to new strategies for reducing the real-time image processing burden in robotic systems, and could also help in training trail runners by emphasizing limber joints when dealing with uneven terrain.
evidence: Speculative application of findings.
